strengths: Interesting empirical motivation: The paper provides empirical and statistical evidence (via subset cosine similarity, CCA, and Pearson correlation) showing that resolution degradation causes a relatively consistent directional shift in feature space.

Simplicity and computational efficiency: VPFA is designed as a post-processing feature alignment module with a frozen backbone, avoiding the need for heavy end-to-end retraining or complex super-resolution GANs, yielding fast inference and low overhead.

Comprehensive exploration of settings: The evaluation extends beyond standard benchmarks to more severe degradation factors (MLRpro), large-scale data (MSMT17), cross-dataset generalization, and cross-modality tasks (visible-infrared and text-image ReID).
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison in Table 3: The proposed method builds upon TransReID (yielding a 3840-dimensional representation), whereas most baseline CR-ReID methods in Table 3 (e.g., PS-HRNet, LRAR, CAD, INTACT) use ResNet-50 or other standard CNN backbones. Table 4a reveals that vanilla TransReID alone already achieves 90.3% Rank-1 on MLR-Market-1501, which is higher than nearly all previous methods in Table 3. Without evaluating baseline methods on TransReID or evaluating VPFA on ResNet-50, it is impossible to decouple the gains of the proposed vector panning from the superiority of the backbone.

Omission of mAP in main benchmarks: Mean Average Precision (mAP) is an essential evaluation metric in the person ReID community, yet Table 3 only reports Rank-1, Rank-5, and Rank-10 for all four primary benchmark datasets.

Handling varying and unknown resolution scales: In the MLR benchmark, query degradation rates vary randomly ($r \in \{2, 3, 4\}$). The paper applies a single static transformation without conditioning on scale or estimating resolution. It is unclear how the model behaves when applied to images with differing or continuous degrees of degradation, or if applied mistakenly to images that are already high-resolution.

Limited technical novelty: Methodologically, VPFA is essentially a 3-layer residual MLP trained with Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss on identity prototype pairs. While the word-embedding analogy is intuitive, the technical mechanism itself is standard feature regression.

Notational and citation inaccuracies: In Algorithm 1, Stage 2(c) states 'Compute loss $L_{VPL}$ using Eq. (2)', whereas Eq. (2) defines prototype averaging and Eq. (6)/(8) defines the loss. In Section 1, the citation 'Neel et al.' is missing a publication year and standard citation syntax.

strengths: The paper is clearly structured and easy to follow, with clean visualizations illustrating the conceptual intuition.
The proposed post-processing module is decoupled from backbone training, making it computationally lightweight during feature transformation.
The authors conduct evaluations across several datasets (Market-1501, CUHK03, VIPeR, CAVIAR, MSMT17) and extend the analysis to cross-modality retrieval settings.
weaknesses: Unfair backbone comparison in the main benchmark: Table 3 compares the proposed method against prior cross-resolution ReID methods (e.g., SING, CSR-GAN, INTACT, LRAR, PS-HRNet) that predominantly use ResNet-50 backbones. However, the proposed method uses a much stronger Transformer backbone (TransReID with 3840-d features). In Table 4a, the baseline TransReID alone without any VPFA module already achieves 90.3% Rank-1 on MLR-Market-1501, which already matches or exceeds almost all previous methods in Table 3 (e.g., LRAR at 90.1%). Thus, the reported superior performance is largely driven by the modern Vision Transformer backbone rather than the proposed feature alignment method.

Limited methodological novelty: The core contribution boils down to training a standard three-layer residual MLP with Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss to map low-resolution features to high-resolution features. Rebranding standard MSE loss as 'Vector Panning Loss (VPL)' and expanding the Euclidean distance via the law of cosines does not provide novel theoretical or algorithmic insight.

Trivial statistical justification: The empirical observation in Table 1 and Section 3—that averaging HR-LR differences across identities yields consistent direction vectors—is a standard consequence of the law of large numbers. Since synthetic downsampling is a deterministic degradation applied across all images, identity-specific variations naturally cancel out when averaged over hundreds of identities, leaving the dataset-level degradation mean shift. Presenting this as an analogy to word2vec semantic arithmetic is conceptually overstated.

Omission of critical evaluation metrics: Standard person ReID literature evaluates performance using both Cumulative Matching Characteristics (CMC Rank-k) and mean Average Precision (mAP). In Table 3, mAP is omitted across all four main CR-ReID benchmark datasets, reporting only Rank-1, Rank-5, and Rank-10.

Misleading efficiency reporting: Section 5.4 claims an inference throughput of '4,424,371.31 samples/second', which exclusively measures running a 3-layer MLP on pre-extracted feature vectors. It ignores the significant computational latency of the TransReID feature extraction backbone, which accounts for virtually all inference runtime in practice.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical issue in person re-identification: handling cross-resolution discrepancies between query and gallery images without computationally expensive super-resolution modules.

The proposed method is lightweight and conceptually simple, functioning as a plug-and-play post-processing MLP adapter on top of frozen backbone features, achieving high throughput during feature transformation.
The manuscript explores cross-dataset and cross-modality (visible-infrared and text-image) settings in the appendix, showing the potential versatility of residual feature adapters.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons: The method uses TransReID (a Vision Transformer backbone) as its feature extractor, whereas virtually all baseline methods in Table 3 (e.g., PS-HRNet, LRAR, CAD, SING, INTACT) are built upon ResNet-50. As shown in the ablation study (Table 4a), the TransReID baseline alone achieves 90.3% Rank-1 on MLR-Market-1501, which already matches or exceeds almost every competing method in Table 3. Without re-evaluating the baselines using TransReID or evaluating VPFA on ResNet-50, it is impossible to attribute the reported state-of-the-art results to the proposed VPFA framework rather than simply to a much stronger backbone.

Limited novelty and overstated terminology: Methodologically, the framework consists of a standard 3-layer MLP trained with Mean Squared Error (MSE) to map LR features to HR features using residual learning. Renaming standard MSE to 'Vector Panning Loss (VPL)' and feature regression to 'Vector Panning' overclaims what is fundamentally a standard residual MLP adapter.

Contradictory claims regarding supervision: Section 4.4 claims that 'Our training requires no ID labels and learns the resolution difference in the vector space' and that the process is 'supervision-free'. However, Section 4.1 (Eq. 2) and Algorithm 1 explicitly require identity annotations to group features by identity and construct identity-level prototype pairs $(z_{LR}^i, z_{HR}^i)$ for supervision.

Dubious interpretation of the 'semantic direction': The observation in Table 1—that difference vectors averaged across all identities in two disjoint subsets have a cosine similarity above 0.99—is largely an artifact of the Law of Large Numbers reflecting the global distribution mean shift (domain shift) between blurred/downsampled images and sharp images, rather than evidence for a discrete word2vec-style analogical vector space.

Lack of practical testing for resolution awareness at inference: In inference, the method assumes it is known a priori which images are LR and need panning. Furthermore, the synthetic benchmark uses multiple downsampling rates (2x, 3x, 4x), but there is little analysis on how VPFA handles varying or continuous resolution scales if the degradation level is unknown or mixed.

Presentation and citation errors: There are several notable errors throughout the text, including citing the foundational Generative Adversarial Nets paper as 'PyrNet(Goodfellow et al. 2014)' in Table 3, typos such as 'retrieval retrieval' (page 2), 'Section Section 3' (page 2), 'CUHK08' instead of 'CUHK03' (page 7), and numerous missing spaces before citations/table references (e.g., 'Table1', 'Table4a', 'Table4bshows').

strengths: Insightful empirical observation: The paper demonstrates that resolution degradation induces a consistent, structured directional shift in the deep feature space rather than arbitrary noise, supported by empirical subset cosine similarities, CCA, and Pearson correlation analyses.

Lightweight and practical design: In contrast to complex super-resolution pipelines (e.g., SRGAN, SwinIR) or cumbersome joint adversarial training schemes, VPFA decouples feature alignment from backbone training. It is a lightweight post-hoc residual MLP that adds minimal compute and runs at over 4 million feature vectors per second during inference.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors conduct extensive evaluations across synthetic (Market-1501, CUHK03, VIPeR, MSMT17) and real-world (CAVIAR) benchmarks, diverse downsampling scales (2x to 7x), multiple backbones (ViT, DeiT, CLIP-ReID CNN), other post-hoc adaptation baselines (FiLM, Adapter, mean offset), and even cross-modality tasks (VI-ReID and TI-ReID).

Thorough ablations, visualizations, and candid discussion of limitations: The paper provides informative t-SNE and Grad-CAM visualizations, cross-dataset transfer experiments, and an honest reflection on the boundaries of feature-space panning.
weaknesses: Overselling standard techniques: The core formulation is essentially a standard 3-layer residual MLP trained with Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss to regress paired high-resolution embeddings from low-resolution embeddings. Introducing terms like 'Vector Panning Loss (VPL)' and expanding Euclidean distance via the law of cosines to claim novelty in aligning direction and magnitude dresses up a conventional MSE regression setup.

Potential backbone confounding in main comparison: In Table 3, the proposed method utilizes a powerful TransReID (ViT) backbone, whereas most published CR-ReID baselines are built on ResNet-50 or custom CNN backbones. The TransReID baseline alone achieves 90.3% Rank-1 on MLR-Market-1501 without any alignment, which is already competitive with or superior to many prior methods. Although the appendix provides cross-backbone comparisons (Table 8), Table 3 would be much fairer if prior methods were evaluated with ViT backbones or if VPFA were directly compared against prior methods on the exact same ResNet-50 backbone under identical training data.

Reliance on synthetic paired data: The module relies on having paired HR and downsampled LR images during training to extract paired feature vectors $(z_{LR}, z_{HR})$. While standard in MLR benchmarks, obtaining clean pairs in arbitrary real-world camera networks with unknown optical degradations and varying viewpoints remains a non-trivial challenge.

Minor presentation issues: In the abstract, the phrase 'Code is available at' is left empty without a repository URL or placeholder. Additionally, citations in the text occasionally lack publication years (e.g., 'Neel et al.' on page 2).

strengths: Insightful conceptual motivation: The paper provides an intriguing empirical and statistical investigation showing that resolution discrepancies in person ReID feature representations exhibit consistent, structured directional shifts across identities (supported by cosine similarity across disjoint subsets, CCA, and Pearson correlation analysis).

Lightweight and practical post-hoc design: The proposed Vector Panning Feature Alignment (VPFA) operates entirely in feature space on top of a frozen backbone, requiring no end-to-end retraining, architectural modification, or computationally heavy image super-resolution modules.

Strong and consistent experimental results: VPFA achieves state-of-the-art performance across four benchmark datasets (MLR-Market-1501, MLR-CUHK03, MLR-VIPeR, and CAVIAR), outperforming both SR-based and resolution-invariant baselines, and shows substantial gains (+3.8% Rank-1) directly over the TransReID baseline.

Comprehensive validation and ablations: The appendix provides extensive supplementary evaluations, including testing across different downsampling ratios, challenging extensions (MLRpro, MSMT17), cross-modality tasks (visible-infrared, text-to-image), multiple backbones (ViT, DeiT, CNN), and comparisons with general post-hoc adaptation techniques (FiLM, Adapters, mean vector offset).
weaknesses: Conceptual tension between 'single resolution direction' and non-linear MLP mapping: The paper motivates the approach through linear semantic offsets (analogous to Mikolov's word embeddings), yet the implemented solution is an input-dependent, 3-layer MLP containing 24M parameters. While the authors briefly acknowledge this in the limitations, the method is fundamentally a non-linear feature regression network rather than simple vector panning along a static direction.

Fairness of backbone comparisons in Table 3: In the main comparison table, VPFA uses a ViT-based TransReID backbone, whereas most published CR-ReID baselines are ResNet-50 or CNN-based. Although Table 4a and Table 8 show respectable within-backbone improvements, the headline comparison in Table 3 conflates the strength of the modern Transformer backbone with the contribution of the VPFA module.

Dependence on synthetic paired data: The method relies on paired HR-LR feature vectors for training, which are synthesized via uniform downsampling. Real-world surveillance scenarios often present composite degradations (e.g., severe motion blur, low-light noise, mixed compression artifacts) where paired clean HR references may not be available or synthetic downsampling fails to reflect true sensor discrepancy.

Minor presentation and citation issues: Citations in the text include incomplete references (e.g., 'DeepMind's recent work (Neel et al.)' without publication year/formal citation in the main text), a repeated word ('perform retrieval retrieval' on page 2), and missing URL text in the abstract ('Code is available at').

strengths: Practical and efficient design: The proposed post-hoc feature adaptation approach decouples cross-resolution alignment from backbone training, avoiding expensive end-to-end retraining or high-resolution image generation pipelines.

Broad empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate on standard CR-ReID datasets (Market-1501, CUHK03, VIPeR, CAVIAR), extended benchmarks (MSMT17, MLRpro), and explore extensions across backbones (ViT, DeiT, CNN) and cross-modality settings in the appendix.

Inclusion of self-critical limitations: Section 7 candidly acknowledges several key constraints, notably that resolution discrepancy cannot be fully captured by a single 1D direction and that the method primarily operates on synthetic bicubic downsampling.
weaknesses: Conceptual disconnect between motivation and methodology: The core premise is that resolution behaves as a consistent linear semantic direction (analogous to word embeddings such as 'King - Man + Woman = Queen'). However, the actual method does not apply a fixed directional vector; it employs a multi-layer nonlinear MLP with LayerNorm, ReLU, Tanh gating, and 24 million parameters. In the appendix (Table 9), a true vector offset baseline lags substantially behind the MLP, showing that the resolution gap is neither purely directional nor linear. The framing thus overstates the 'direction' insight when the implementation is essentially learning a high-capacity nonlinear feature regressor.

Over-branding of standard techniques: The paper renames standard machine learning components with bespoke terminology. Specifically, Section 4.3 defines 'Vector Panning Loss (VPL)', which the manuscript explicitly notes is mathematically identical to Mean Squared Error (MSE) on paired embeddings. A three-layer residual MLP trained with MSE loss between paired source and target features is an established regression baseline, and packaging it as a fundamentally new framework overclaims novelty.

Confounded benchmark comparisons in Table 3: In the main comparison table, VPFA is built upon a modern Transformer backbone (TransReID / ViT), whereas the vast majority of competing CR-ReID methods in Table 3 are based on older ResNet-50 architectures. As revealed in the ablation study (Table 4a), the TransReID baseline alone achieves 90.3% Rank-1 on MLR-Market-1501 without any VPFA module, which already outperforms almost every baseline in Table 3. Comparing VPFA against ResNet-based methods without re-benchmarking those prior approaches on the same ViT backbone makes it difficult to separate architectural advantages from the true contribution of the VP module.

Questionable statistical validation: The high cosine similarity (>0.99) reported in Table 1 between average difference vectors of disjoint subsets is largely expected when applying uniform synthetic bicubic downsampling across an image dataset; averaging over thousands of samples isolates the global low-pass filtering effect across the dataset. Furthermore, the CCA results in Table 2a show only moderate canonical correlations (~0.48) between identical pedestrian images that differ merely by downsampling.

Unclear training formulation on real-world datasets: In synthetic datasets, pairs are trivially constructed via downsampling the same image. However, for real datasets such as CAVIAR where HR and LR images come from different cameras and capture different poses/lighting, the paper does not sufficiently explain how exact paired samples {(z_LR, z_HR)} are chosen to train the module without introducing cross-pose and cross-view noise into the MSE objective.
